title: Small acts
hook: love is mostly in small things

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Queen Mallika, who said no one was dearer to her than herself. Your line was me too.

Drip. Drip. A leaky faucet over a bucket, or rain off the edge of a roof into a clay pot. Each drop is almost nothing. Nobody would bother to measure one. Leave the pot there overnight, though, and in the morning it's full to the brim. A verse in the Dhammapada, an old collection of the Buddha's sayings, uses exactly that picture, and not for water. For goodness. Three traditions speak to how small love can be and still count.
screen: `DRIP. DRIP.` → `EACH DROP IS ALMOST NOTHING.` → `IN THE MORNING, A FULL POT.`

segments.voice: First, the water-pot. In Max Müller's translation of the Dhammapada, the verse warns against thinking lightly of good, as if it could never add up to much. Then comes the picture: "Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled." The wise, it says, become full of good the same way, gathering it little by little. No single drop fills the pot; every drop is part of the filling. Second, a cup of water. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus says that whoever gives "a cup of cold water only" to one of his little ones, in the name of a disciple, "shall in no wise lose his reward." Notice the word only. Not a banquet. Not a fortune. Just water, and cold, which in a hot land is its own kindness. Third, a face. A saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, recorded in the collection of al-Tirmidhi, says in plain words that your smile in the face of your brother is charity. So, in the same saying, is guiding someone who is lost, or moving a stone out of the road. Charity, here, isn't only money. Fourth, what the three share, each in its own words. None of them says big acts don't matter. They say small ones aren't nothing. A text back. A door held. The dishes done without being asked. On an ordinary day, love often looks like that, and these teachers say it adds up.
screen: `A WATER-POT, DROP BY DROP.` · `A CUP OF COLD WATER ONLY.` · `A SMILE IS CHARITY.` · `SMALL ISN'T NOTHING.` · then, large: `SMALL ACTS.`

segments.voice: Breathe slowly and let the day ahead come to mind, the places you'll be and the people you'll see, and find three small kindnesses that fit inside it: a glass of water poured for someone, a real smile at the counter, a message that says thinking of you. See each one clearly, one at a time, the way a drop falls. If you pray, you can offer the day in your own tradition's words.
Small acts. Kindnesses too small to measure one by one, the drop, the cup of water, the smile, that fill the pot over time. Today's word.
Your line: small things. Nobody needs to measure the drops for the pot to fill. That's day eight hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Buddhists speak of gathering merit little by little through everyday good deeds, Christians read the cup of cold water as a picture of small service, and the hadith in al-Tirmidhi counts a smile or removing harm from a path among acts of charity.

chat.says: What's the point of tiny kindnesses? They hardly change anything.
options: They add up: the Dhammapada says even falling drops will fill a water-pot.
Only big acts truly count; small ones are too little to make a difference.
Small kindnesses only count as charity when money is involved in them.
chat.meaning: The Dhammapada's pot fills drop by drop, Matthew's cup of cold water isn't lost, and in the hadith a smile counts as charity.
